part_title: GenAI Capacity Management: Target Tracking, Predictive Scaling and Guardrails

scenes.title: Management and governance for GenAI workloads
scenes.narration: This overview shows four operating loops around one generative AI application, and each loop answers a different question. The capacity loop uses AWS scaling controls to respond when request demand rises or falls. The spend loop uses Cost Explorer and Cost Anomaly Detection to understand whether infrastructure and model activity cost more than expected. The observability loop connects metrics, logs and traces into Managed Grafana dashboards so operators can investigate latency, failures and bottlenecks. Finally, the operations loop uses Systems Manager to apply configuration, patches and scripts to managed infrastructure. Notice that the charts are illustrative: their values are examples rather than recommended limits. A dashboard that reveals rising P-ninety-five model latency is not itself an automatic scaling or remediation policy. Similarly, a cost anomaly alert does not shut down resources. For production AI systems, define which signals trigger a human investigation, which safe actions may run automatically and which require change approval. Treat demand, cost, visibility and operational hygiene as complementary responsibilities.

scenes.title: Scaling responsibilities across AWS
scenes.narration: Compare the four services by the resource each one changes. EC2 Auto Scaling adjusts the number of virtual machines in an Auto Scaling group. Application Auto Scaling can change the desired capacity of supported applications, including certain ECS service task counts. DynamoDB scaling adjusts provisioned read or write capacity when applicable, although on-demand mode follows a different capacity model. Aurora Auto Scaling can add or remove supported reader instances; that is not the same as automatically enlarging a primary writer. The illustrative metrics show CPU and provisioned-capacity utilisation triggering changes. A target percentage cannot be transplanted blindly between a database and an inference worker. Evaluate the relevant bottleneck and the scaling latency for each service. The lower note calls out Spot interruption risk: checkpoint work, use retries and spread capacity across suitable zones and instance types. For a GenAI application, adding ECS tasks may increase request handling capacity but does not increase an external model's Bedrock quota. Scaling is always constrained by the slowest dependent resource.

scenes.title: Target tracking: automatic scaling to a metric target
scenes.narration: This slide follows a target-tracking policy over time. The example sets an illustrative fifty-percent average CPU utilisation target, along with minimum and maximum capacity. When the incoming load raises CPU above that target, the policy adds instances or tasks. Once the extra capacity becomes healthy, each worker carries less load and the metric approaches the target. Later, if demand drops sufficiently, the policy can remove capacity after the relevant stabilisation periods. The lower diagrams show why scaling is not instantaneous: new resources need launch, application startup, health checks and metric propagation. Warmup and scale-in controls help prevent oscillation or premature removal. Minimum capacity preserves a baseline, while maximum capacity limits exposure to runaway cost and scaling beyond dependent-service quotas. The right metric matters as much as the number: CPU might be useful for a CPU-bound API, while queue backlog per worker can be better for batch inference. Test the metric against actual throughput and user-visible latency instead of treating fifty percent as an AWS universal optimum.

scenes.title: Scaling plans and predictive scaling
scenes.narration: The architecture brings together historical demand, scheduled changes and reactive scaling. A scaling plan can coordinate policies across supported resource types, but the right native scaling feature still depends on the resource and current AWS service support. Predictive scaling uses sufficient historical patterns to anticipate recurring EC2 demand and arrange capacity before the expected peak. Scheduled scaling handles known events, such as a planned promotion, while target tracking responds when real traffic diverges from forecasts. The illustrated graph compares predicted demand, actual demand and capacity across several days. No prediction is guaranteed, and a one-off event may not resemble previous traffic. Avoid assuming two weeks of history is an absolute rule for all configurations; verify the current service's requirements. For GenAI inference, the deployment may need additional warmup for model loading, GPU readiness and endpoint health. Plan capacity arrival around those realities, cap the fleet and monitor forecast error. Use predictive and reactive mechanisms together only where their interaction is understood and supported.

scenes.title: Scaling guardrails for AI applications
scenes.narration: Follow the incoming documents and prompts into a work queue, then to worker containers that invoke Amazon Bedrock. The queue decouples arrival rate from processing capacity. Rather than scaling only on CPU, a consumer fleet can target the amount of backlog per worker, with an appropriate threshold and safety range determined from processing duration. The slide's figures for desired workers and backlog are illustrative. The next constraint is model-provider quotas: requests per minute, tokens per minute and concurrent operations may limit useful inference even if you add more containers. Set explicit maximum and minimum capacity and integrate budget or cost alarms, but recognise that alarms only stop spend if an actual control is configured. Long-running generations need work-aware scale-in protection or graceful draining so tasks are not terminated mid-request. Retry throttled calls with backoff and preserve idempotency when queue messages are redelivered. The goal is to scale actual useful throughput while respecting cost, availability and the downstream model limits.
